stated_mechanism: Intra-abdominal pressure during retching disrupts fresh anastomoses and wound closure.

Charaka Siddhisthana 2 names the Vriddha among those not to be given emesis, and Charaka Vimanasthana 8.122 places Jirna (old age) from 60. Retching raises intrathoracic and arterial pressure in a vasculature that no longer buffers it.
As Atidurbala — Vamana in a depleted patient causes Dhatu Kshaya.
Forceful retching can tear the gastro-oesophageal junction (Mallory-Weiss); on an anticoagulant the bleed does not stop.
Extreme depletion — as underweight.
Vagal surge during forceful emesis can provoke arrhythmia in an already unstable rhythm.
Raktapitta. Retching raises intrathoracic pressure and risks Mallory-Weiss tearing that will not clot.

Vomiting or purgation loses doses of a drug with a narrow window — too little and a transplanted organ is rejected; dehydration with too much and the kidney is poisoned. Levels must be checked by the transplant team before any expulsive Karma.
The KB lists children under 12 as absolute for Vamana. The forceful Vega and the volume of milk or Yashtimadhu decoction given to fill the stomach are adult quantities for an adult oesophagus.
Emesis after a large fluid load swings volume and electrolytes; a diseased kidney has no reserve, and acute kidney injury follows.

Vomiting with insulin on board is the textbook trigger of diabetic ketoacidosis, and the fasting Snehapana before it a hypoglycaemia window. Vamana induces both on purpose in a patient with no insulin of their own.
Emesis depletes potassium, and hypokalaemia is the commonest precipitant of digoxin toxicity and arrhythmia.
Atidurbala — as underweight.
The vomiting reflex and the associated Valsalva can precipitate a seizure; the KB lists active epilepsy as absolute.
Oesophageal varices, strictures and motility disorders all tear or obstruct under forceful emesis.
Same mechanism as severe cardiac disease; the KB lists severe cardiac disease as an absolute contraindication.
Fluid shifts from 8 glasses of pre-emetic liquid followed by rapid loss can precipitate decompensation.
As bleeding disorder — an oesophageal tear during emesis is uncontrollable.
Forceful retching raises intra-abdominal pressure — the mechanism by which a hernia enlarges or strangulates.
Emesis against a herniated gastro-oesophageal junction risks strangulation and severe reflux injury.
The KB lists severe hypertension as ABSOLUTE for Vamana, not relative. Each retch spikes systolic pressure; the engine previously treated this as a soft warning and proceeded.
Emesis and the fluid lost with it concentrate lithium, whose toxic level sits close to its therapeutic one.

Active SLE is a Dhatu Kshaya state, and serositis or pulmonary involvement makes the repeated Valsalva of emesis dangerous. Conservative by intent — SLE ranges from mild to organ-threatening and this layer cannot tell which.
Emetic drugs and the fluid loss of Vamana both reach the infant through breast milk.
Gastric acid driven repeatedly across an ulcerated mucosa risks perforation and bleeding.
Forceful emesis raises intra-abdominal pressure and risks placental abruption and preterm labour.
Emesis demands respiratory reserve and carries aspiration risk into lungs that have none; hypoxia during repeated retching is not recoverable by breathing harder.
Oesophageal dysmotility and stricture are near-universal in systemic sclerosis; forceful emesis against a fibrosed oesophagus risks perforation, and impaired clearance makes aspiration likely.
Repeated Valsalva during emesis causes sharp swings in venous return and blood pressure that a failing heart cannot buffer.
The fluid loss of Vamana haemoconcentrates the blood, which is the classic precipitant of a vaso-occlusive crisis.
Atidurbala. Vamana costs Bala the emaciated patient does not have; the KB lists Atidurbala as absolute.
The label is not a recognised diagnosis, but what it reports is low reserve, and that is what is acted on here: treat as reduced Bala and use the mildest effective dose.
A dose vomited is a dose lost. Time the anti-epileptic after the emesis has fully settled and never skip it — a missed dose is a seizure risk.
After the fluid lost in emesis, the usual dose can drop the pressure too far — rise slowly, and have the pressure checked before standing.
A dose vomited is a dose missed — an 'off' period follows. The prescriber plans the dose around the Karma day.
Retching on an antiplatelet can provoke an oozing gastric or oesophageal bleed; report any blood in the vomitus at once.
Vamana is a frightening procedure; the KB names severe psychological fragility as relative. Sattvavajaya preparation is required first.
As COPD — aspiration and bronchospasm risk while retching against narrowed airways.
An expulsive Karma is a large exertion; post-exertional malaise can follow for days. Mridu dose, and rest is part of the course.
Vamana is classically indicated for Kapha in the chest, so this is not a bar — but an acute Pratishyaya is not the moment to begin a multi-week course. Let the acute phase settle first.
Retching under a fluid load risks aspiration and bronchospasm in obstructed airways; check oxygen saturation before and during.
Long-term steroids blunt the adrenal response to physiological stress, and Vamana is one. Never stop the steroid for the course; the prescriber may need to cover the Karma day.
Emesis on top of a diuretic compounds fluid and potassium loss; the prescriber should review the dose for the Karma and Samsarjana days.
As chronic fatigue — the exertion of Vamana can set off a flare lasting beyond the course.
Reflux is aggravated for days afterwards; use the mildest Madanaphala dose and extend Samsarjana Krama.
Retching is a sustained Valsalva and raises intraocular pressure sharply; ophthalmologist clearance first.
Levothyroxine taken that morning is vomited with the Kapha, and the dose is lost. Move the tablet to the evening for the Karma day and the days around it.
Vomiting within three hours of a pill counts as a missed pill. Use a barrier method until seven pills after the course.
Shodhana is a deliberate physiological stress; on immunosuppression, infection after the Karma presents late and quietly. Coordinate with the prescriber.

The Karma day and the Peya/Vilepi days after it are close to a fast, and the drug lowers glucose whether or not food arrives — the classic setting for a hypoglycaemic collapse. The prescribing doctor must set the dose for these days before the course begins; carry glucose.
Each retch spikes venous and intraocular pressure. In neovascular (wet) AMD this risks a subretinal bleed — obtain ophthalmology clearance before proceeding.
Emesis during an attack is indistinguishable from the attack; the vertigo makes falls likely and can extend the episode. Schedule only between attacks.
Vomiting and dehydration with metformin risk lactic acidosis and acute kidney injury; the sick-day rule is to pause it while vomiting, which only the prescriber can authorise.
Forceful retching flexes the thoracic spine under load; in severe osteoporosis that is the mechanism of a vertebral compression fracture.
Loss of bodily control during emesis is a common trigger. Prepare with Sattvavajaya and stop at the patient's word.

Fasting and fluid loss on an SGLT2 inhibitor can tip into euglycaemic ketoacidosis with a normal glucose reading. Sick-day rules apply: the prescriber normally withholds it from the day before the Karma until eating is normal.
The airway is already prone to collapse; emesis needs it held open and protected, so the procedure requires positioning and observation it does not normally get.
Chronic anaemia is reduced Bala; use the mildest emetic, and not at all if transfusion-dependent.
A tablet vomited within hours is not absorbed. Take it once the Vamana day has settled, as the prescriber directs.
The head-down posture and repeated retching provoke vestibular symptoms, and the weakness (Klama) after Vamana makes a fall likely. An attendant stays throughout.
Pandu. Purgation depletes further in a patient already short of Rakta Dhatu; carried over from the engine's original set.
Extreme depletion — as underweight.
Raktapitta. Repeated purgation abrades the mucosa in a patient who cannot clot.

Vomiting or purgation loses doses of a drug with a narrow window — too little and a transplanted organ is rejected; dehydration with too much and the kidney is poisoned. Levels must be checked by the transplant team before any expulsive Karma.

Levodopa is absorbed in the small intestine on a timed schedule; purgation cuts the dose actually absorbed, and a missed dose brings an 'off' period of rigidity and falls. Keep the dosing times; the prescriber decides any change.
As heart disease — hypokalaemia and dehydration after purgation raise the ventricular rate and destabilise rate control.
Chronic malabsorption means lower reserve and slower recovery; the Samsarjana Krama itself is rice and dal and so is safe, but the purgation compounds an existing deficit.

Purgation depletes fluid and electrolytes in a patient whose reserve is the problem; Mridu dose and a longer Samsarjana.
Fluid and electrolyte shifts are poorly tolerated; mild dose with close monitoring only.

Reduced Bala and slower fluid compensation — mild dose, extended Samsarjana.

As chronic fatigue — dehydration and exertion can set off a flare. Mridu dose.
Purgation flushes levothyroxine taken that morning before it is absorbed; separate the dose from the Karma day.
Purgation moves potassium and fluid out quickly; low potassium provokes arrhythmia in a diseased heart. Electrolytes before and after.

NSAIDs with purgation-induced dehydration risk acute kidney injury, and they irritate a gut already purged.

Purgation is fluid loss; on an SGLT2 inhibitor that risks ketoacidosis with a normal glucose. Sick-day rules: the prescriber normally withholds it until eating and drinking are normal.
These medicines cause low sodium (SIADH), most in the elderly; purgation and the large water intake around it add to it.
Chronic anaemia is reduced Bala; the fluid loss is tolerated poorly.
Purgation shortens gut transit and cuts levothyroxine absorption; keep at least four hours between the tablet and the purgative.

Niruha is given on an empty stomach and contains honey; the combination of a fasting procedure and an evacuant with a sugar in it is the glucose swing the soft entry warns about. Anuvasana/Matra Basti is given after food.

Active nasal bleeding — instillation obscures and worsens the source.

Wait for resolution — the KB and the contraindication matrix both defer Shodhana during Jwara.
